timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I keep seeing MITRE ATT&CK mentioned everywhere. What exactly is it?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: MITRE ATT&CK is a comprehensive matrix of every known attacker technique, organized by tactics - the 'why' - and techniques - the 'how.' It's like a periodic table for cyber attacks.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly. Tactics are the goals: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Exfiltration, and Impact. Techniques are how each goal is achieved.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: For example, Initial Access has techniques like Phishing (T1566), Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), and Valid Accounts (T1078). Each technique has sub-techniques, detection guidance, and mitigations.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: How do security teams actually use this?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Three main ways: threat intelligence mapping - every APT report maps to ATT&CK techniques; detection engineering - you build detection rules for each technique; and gap analysis - you identify which techniques you can't detect.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: ATT&CK Navigator lets you visualize your detection coverage. Create a heat map showing which techniques you detect, which you partially detect, and which are blind spots. It's sobering.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Atomic Red Team provides test cases for each technique - you can verify your detections work. Sigma rules map to ATT&CK for SIEM detection. And tools like Mallory and Breach & Attack Simulation platforms continuously test your coverage.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: name the ATT&CK tactics in order, give examples of techniques for at least 5 tactics, and explain how you'd use ATT&CK for detection engineering. This separates junior from senior candidates.
